title: Cotopaxi Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cotopaxi wells have a 125-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $14,100-$24,500.
h1: What Wells Are Like Around Cotopaxi, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land near Cotopaxi means dealing mostly with mountain bedrock, not a broad Denver Basin aquifer. Records within 5 miles show a 125-foot median well depth, but local drilling can vary substantially. The middle half runs from 75 to 240 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 900 feet.

Most permitted wells serve domestic or household uses, and the named aquifer is usually unnamed fractured bedrock. The well records are useful for setting expectations, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will produce on a particular parcel. Nearby wells, access, geology, septic layout and the intended use all matter.

sections.heading: Cotopaxi well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Around Cotopaxi, the typical permitted well is 125 feet deep. The middle half of recorded depths runs from 75 to 240 feet, while the 90th percentile is 335 feet. About 33% are under 100 feet, 51% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 13% between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet.

That spread is normal for a fractured granite and gneiss setting. Water can travel through individual fractures rather than a consistent, continuous layer. A driller may need to continue well below nearby shallow wells if the first fractures do not provide enough water. For a bid, use the 125-foot median as a starting point, not a promised completion depth. Ask how costs change if the hole reaches the deeper local range.

sections.heading: Most Cotopaxi wells produce usable household rates
sections.html:
Among the 286 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 6.0 to 13.0 gallons per minute. About 64% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 19% report more than 15 gallons per minute. A smaller share, 15%, reports 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution is encouraging for ordinary household use, but a pump-yield record is not the same as a guaranteed long-term supply. Low-yield wells may still work with adequate storage and careful demand planning. Confirm the permit’s allowed use, test the well after construction, and match the water system to the home, livestock or irrigation plans.

sections.heading: The Cotopaxi water-level record is fairly steady
sections.html:
Of the permitted wells, 68 report a static water level. The median depth to water is 74 feet, with the middle half from 48 to 132 feet below the surface. This affects pump placement, trenching and the amount of water a pump must lift, but the measurement is specific to each well and its measurement conditions.

The decade comparison does not show a clear dropping trend in this record set. The median static level was 81 feet below ground in the 2010s and 80 feet in the 2020s. That small difference should not be treated as a site guarantee. A buyer still needs the actual neighboring well logs and a current test where water supply is important.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use around Cotopaxi
sections.html:
Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records include 721 wells within the mapped area, with 469 recorded as constructed. Permits span from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The busiest decade was the 1990s, with 189 permits; the 1980s had 120, the 2010s had 98, and the 2000s had 83.

American Drilling Service, associated in the records with Dewberry, Bradford W., appears most often with 156 wells. American Drilling Service Inc., associated with Dewberry, Noble, appears with 76. Owner records account for 34. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Check the actual construction record, casing, grout, yield and static level rather than relying only on who drilled nearby wells.

sections.heading: A median-depth Cotopaxi well costs more than drilling alone
sections.html:
In this fractured mountain bedrock, a planning rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 125-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $8,100 to $12,500. A finished system including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical models to about $14,100 to $24,500.

The final invoice can move outside that range if the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grouting requirements change, or the site needs longer utility trenches. Ask for a written breakdown separating drilling from completion equipment and site work. A shallow neighboring well does not establish your drilling depth, especially where water depends on fractured granite or gneiss.

sections.heading: Mines, septic layout and low-yield risk need checking
sections.html:
The mapped area around Cotopaxi includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 99 historic mine features within about 10 miles. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those facts do not prove contamination at a specific parcel, but they are reasons to review environmental records and test private well water before relying on it.

Low yield and dry-hole risk remain possible in fractured bedrock even though the reported yield median is 10.0 gallons per minute. Septic setbacks, well access, building placement and room for a pump system should be reviewed before excavation. A domestic well is generally intended for household use under its permit, not unrestricted irrigation or expanded development. Confirm water rights and any augmentation requirement with DWR.

sections.heading: What to verify before buying near Cotopaxi
sections.html:
Start with the well permit and construction report for the property, then compare nearby records in Cotopaxi, Coaldale and Howard. Look for depth, casing, grout, reported yield and static water level. The area’s 125-foot median and 75-to-240-foot middle range can help evaluate a bid, but the local fracture pattern controls the result.

Before closing, arrange a current water-quality test and a production or recovery test appropriate to the property’s intended use. Confirm that the permit matches the planned home and occupants, and ask whether stock, irrigation or additional buildings create a water-rights issue. If building, place the well, septic system, driveway and house together on a site plan so access and required separation can be maintained.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cotopaxi, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth near Cotopaxi is 125 feet. The middle half runs from 75 to 240 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 335 feet and the deepest recorded well is 900 feet. Because the area is fractured granite and gneiss, nearby wells can have very different depths even on similar mountain parcels.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cotopaxi?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 125-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,100 to $12,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $14,100 to $24,500. A deeper hole or difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Cotopaxi?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 6.0 to 13.0 gallons per minute. About 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 64% are in the 5-to-15 range. These records are useful for comparison, but they do not guarantee a new well’s production.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cotopaxi?
faq.a: A private well should be tested rather than assumed safe. The area has 4 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 99 historic mine features within about 10 miles, although there are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water for applicable contaminants, and repeat testing when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are Cotopaxi wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available static-level record does not show a clear dropping trend. Median depth to water was 81 feet below ground in the 2010s and 80 feet in the 2020s. Only 68 wells report static levels, so that comparison is limited. Review the specific well’s recovery, production and neighboring well history before buying.
